raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old Japanese man with no symptoms had a positive fecal occult blood test. His past medical history included a duodenal ulcer at 50 years of age.
The colonoscopy revealed, in the observation range, many scars caused by inflammation in the cecum and ascending colon, an intestinal stricture caused by inflammatory polyps in the transverse colon (Figure 1A-D), loss of both visible vascular patterns and haustra in the descending colon (Figure 1E), and normal mucosa in the sigmoid colon (Figure 1F), rectum, and ileum. Examination of biopsies from each segment of colon (including even specimens from normal mucosa) revealed chronic colitis accompanied by IS, as evidenced by basophilic fringes on the luminal surface of the intestinal mucosa and infiltration of lymphocytes and eosinophils in subepithelial lesions (Figure 2A). There were no obvious dysplastic changes (Figure 2B). Abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed wall thickening in the transverse colon around the hepatic flexure (Figure 3A). The upper endoscopy and enteroscopy findings were within normal limits. Laboratory data, including carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA), purified protein derivative skin test, Entamoeba histolytica antibody, human immunodeficiency virus antibody, and fecal examinations, including culture and polymerase chain reaction for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, revealed no remarkable findings. Hence, his condition was diagnosed as chronic colitis associated with IS. Metronidazole (MNZ) 1500 mg/d for 14 days was initiated to treat the IS. Although spirochetes were eliminated in pathological examinations, MNZ was not effective for the intestinal stricture of the transverse colon. We performed colonoscopy 4 times for 20 months since the fecal occult blood test was positive and each biopsy indicated colitis but no obvious malignancy (Figure 2C, Table 1).
The patient was admitted to our hospital with an acute abdomen 20 months after the initial presentation. He had urgent abdominal pain, constipation, and fever. Abdominal CT revealed exacerbation of the intestinal stricture in the transverse colon around the hepatic flexure (Figure 3B) and dilatation of the ascending colon with extraintestinal fluid (Figure 3C). We strongly suspected intestinal perforation due to obstruction. Subtotal colectomy and ileostomy were performed and the symptoms resolved. Histopathological examination of the specimens revealed MC that had infiltrated into the muscularis propia and subserous layers of the visceral peritoneum, purulent peritonitis due to perforation within the tumor and lymph node metastasis (Figure 4). The final histopathological diagnosis was a pT4a (invasion of serosa of peritoneum), pN1 (1/12), Ly0, V0, M0, and R0 tumor, corresponding to the Union for International Cancer Control IIIB classification. An immunohistochemical stain for DNA MMR proteins, including MLH1, MSH2, PMS2, and MSH6, revealed no lack of these expressions (Figure 5). Intensified adjuvant chemotherapy according to the Xeloda (capecitabine) and oxaliplatin schema was initiated. Currently, after 14 months of follow-up, the patient is without detectable tumor recurrence, as shown by abdominal CT scan and ultrasound examination (Table 1).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old initially asymptomatic Japanese male was evaluated for a positive fecal occult blood test and later presented 20 months afterward with an acute abdomen characterized by urgent abdominal pain, constipation, and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially underwent diagnostic colonoscopy for an asymptomatic positive fecal occult blood test, was diagnosed with chronic colitis associated with intestinal spirochetosis (IS) and a transverse colon stricture, and received metronidazole (1500 mg/day for 14 days). Despite eradication of spirochetes on four surveillance colonoscopies over 20 months, the transverse colon stricture persisted, and at 20 months he presented emergently with acute abdominal pain, constipation, and fever.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of duodenal ulcer at age 50 years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initially asymptomatic at index presentation; at 20-month readmission, positive for urgent abdominal pain, constipation, and fever.

objective.physical_examination: At 20-month readmission, clinical signs of an acute abdomen with fever.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline laboratory workup: positive fecal occult blood test (FOBT); serum CEA, CA 19-9, tuberculosis IGRA, PPD skin test, anti-Entamoeba histolytica antibody, and HIV antibody were all negative/normal. Stool cultures and fecal Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial colonoscopy showed inflammatory scarring in the cecum and ascending colon, a transverse colon stricture with inflammatory polyps, loss of vascular pattern and haustra in the descending colon, and normal ileum, sigmoid, and rectum; segmental colonic biopsies showed chronic colitis with subepithelial lymphocytic/eosinophilic infiltration and luminal basophilic fringes diagnostic of intestinal spirochetosis without dysplasia. Upper endoscopy and enteroscopy were normal. Initial abdominal CT showed transverse colon wall thickening near the hepatic flexure. Four surveillance colonoscopies over 20 months showed persistent colitis without spirochetes or biopsy-proven malignancy. At 20 months, emergency abdominal CT demonstrated severe progression of the hepatic-flexure transverse colon stricture, ascending colon dilatation, and extraintestinal fluid suggestive of perforation, prompting emergency subtotal colectomy with ileostomy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Histopathological examination of the resected subtotal colectomy specimen revealed mucinous adenocarcinoma (pT4a pN1 [1/12] Ly0 V0 M0 R0, UICC Stage IIIB; intact MMR proteins MLH1, MSH2, PMS2, MSH6 on immunohistochemistry) infiltrating the visceral peritoneal serosa with intratumoral perforation and purulent peritonitis, arising in the setting of chronic colitis and prior metronidazole-treated intestinal spirochetosis (with amoebiasis and intestinal tuberculosis ruled out). Following subtotal colectomy with ileostomy and resolution of acute symptoms, the patient received adjuvant XELOX (capecitabine and oxaliplatin) chemotherapy and remained free of tumor recurrence on CT and ultrasound at 14-month follow-up.
